peso performed well vs other emerging market currencies despite dollar appreciation","dates":["2021-2022"],"quantities":["over 6 percent spread vs US"],"excerpt":"Banxico's quick response to rising inflation pressures pushed the interest rate spread versus the U.S. to over 6 percent, close to previous highs in the past decade or so.","locator":"page 71","attribution":"International Monetary Fund (IMF) Staff Report, Mexico Article IV Consultation","period_fit":"The data and charts indicate this covers the period since June 2021 through 2022.","source_limitations":["IMF staff calculations based on Bloomberg data","Carry trade attractiveness shows little correlation with actual currency performance across peers"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0002","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Pension funds became the biggest holders of domestic Mexican government securities in mid-2020, replacing foreigners who had been reducing holdings since early 2015.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexican pension funds","action":"bought domestic government securities, became biggest holders","mechanism":"pension fund investment allocation","outcome":"Domestic investors filled the gap left by foreigners; pension funds became the biggest holders by mid-2020","dates":["mid-2020","since early 2015"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"Pension funds in particular have been buying domestic government securities and became the biggest holders in mid-2020.","locator":"page 72","attribution":"International Monetary Fund (IMF) Staff Report, Mexico Article IV Consultation","period_fit":"IMF estimated pension funds could grow from 20% of GDP in 2020 to 35-56% of GDP by 2040.","source_limitations":["Historical data from Haver Analytics; IMF staff calculations"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.4"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0003","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Urban poverty in Mexico increased from 36.8% of households in 2018 to 40.1% in 2020, while rural poverty declined modestly from 57.7% to 56.8% over the same period.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"adverse","actor":"Mexican households / CONEVAL","action":"experienced poverty increase in urban areas and modest improvement in rural areas","mechanism":"COVID-19 pandemic illness and public health restrictions affecting the economy","outcome":"Urban poverty rose to 40.1% by 2020; rural poverty showed modest improvement","dates":["2018","2020"],"quantities":["36.8% urban households in 2018","40.1% urban households in 2020","57.7% rural population in 2018","56.8% rural population in 2020"],"excerpt":"By the end of 2020, rural poverty had posted a modest improvement, with around 56.8 percent of the rural population in poverty or extreme poverty compared to 57.7 percent in 2018. However, the same period also saw a deterioration of conditions in urban areas, with around 40.1 percent of urban households estimated to be in some form of poverty—up from 36.8 percent in 2018.","locator":"page 73","attribution":"CONEVAL (Mexico's National Council for the Evaluation of Social Development Policy), as cited in IMF Staff Report","period_fit":"Data covers 2018-2020; poverty data preceded the 2022 inflation surge being evaluated.","source_limitations":["CONEVAL official measurement using basic basket of necessities as poverty line; urban deterioration attributed to COVID-19 illness and restrictions"],"question_ids":["5B.8","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0004","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"The Mexican government launched the PACIC anti-inflation package in May 2022 with fuel subsidies costing an estimated MEX$395.4 billion (1.4% of GDP) and food-related measures adding further costs, for a total of MEX$541.2 billion (1.86% of GDP).","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government / SHCP","action":"launched Paquete Contra La Inflación y La Carestía (PACIC) anti-inflation package","mechanism":"fuel subsidies; agricultural support programs; price agreements with retailers; tariff reductions","outcome":"Package of measures deployed to mitigate rising inflation impact on households","dates":["May 2022"],"quantities":["MEX$395.4 billion fuel subsidies (1.4% of GDP)","MEX$541.2 billion total (1.86% of GDP)","0.25% of GDP for food price policies","0.10% of GDP for Sowing Life (Sembrando Vida)"],"excerpt":"As the effects of rising inflation began to hit households in early 2022, the Mexican government launched a package of measures to mitigate the impact under the name Paquete Contra La Inflación y La Carestía (PACIC) in May. Fuel subsidies lie at the heart of PACIC and are expected to cost the Federal government around MEX$395.4 billion (1.4 percent of GDP) by the end the year.","locator":"page 74","attribution":"SHCP (Mexico's Ministry of Finance and Public Credit), as cited in IMF Staff Report","period_fit":"Directly relevant to 2022 period under evaluation.","source_limitations":["Budgetary cost estimates from SHCP; policy has no fiscal or regulatory implications for government per agreement with retailers"],"question_ids":["5B.7","5B.8","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0005","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Windfall oil export revenues of approximately MEX$397.8 billion offset the MEX$395.4 billion fuel subsidy cost in 2022, but higher refining margins could make future subsidy costs exceed oil revenue gains.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government / oil export sector","action":"received increased oil revenues while subsidizing domestic fuel costs","mechanism":"oil price increases benefiting export revenues; fuel subsidy mechanism compensating for price differences","outcome":"Oil export windfall approximately matched fuel subsidy costs in 2022, but crack spread spikes could break the offset","dates":["2022"],"quantities":["MEX$397.8 billion oil revenue windfall","MEX$395.4 billion fuel subsidy cost","Windfall gain roughly equals subsidy cost, suggesting net near-zero fiscal impact"],"excerpt":"While domestic fuel subsidies are expected to cost MEX$395.4 billion, the windfall gain in oil revenues relative to the 2022 budget approved in 2021 is estimated at MEX$397.8 billion, suggesting that oil exports can cover the costs of the subsidy scheme.","locator":"page 74","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations, as cited in IMF Staff Report","period_fit":"Relevant to 2022 fiscal year.","source_limitations":["IMF staff estimates; if refining margins spike sharply, subsidy could exceed revenue gain, requiring expenditure adjustment"],"question_ids":["5B.3","5B.9"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0006","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Fuel subsidies reduced Mexico's headline inflation by about 2 percentage points at their June 2022 peak (when subsidies reached 30% of fuel prices), though the direct effect had fallen to 0.2% by late 2022 as global fuel prices declined.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican government / Banxico","action":"provided fuel subsidies to contain retail fuel prices","mechanism":"subsidy mechanism reducing retail fuel prices below market levels","outcome":"Headline inflation reduced by ~2 percentage points at peak; effect diminished to 0.2% as fuel prices fell","dates":["June 2022 (peak)","late 2022 (diminished)"],"quantities":["30% subsidy at peak","2 percentage point reduction in headline inflation at peak","0.2% direct contribution to containing inflation by late 2022","Fuel represents ~6% of consumption basket"],"excerpt":"Peaking in June, subsidies reduced prices by as much as 30 percent. With fuel at about 6 percent of the consumption basket, the direct effects of the fuel subsidy reduced headline inflation by about two percentage points, when it would have peaked at nearly 10 percent.","locator":"page 75","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations, as cited in IMF Staff Report","period_fit":"Directly relevant to 2022 period.","source_limitations":["Estimate may be a lower bound given second-round effects on distribution costs and transport; falling fuel prices since early summer reduced the subsidy effect"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0007","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexican government scaled up pre-existing food security programs (Sembrando Vida, Producción para el Bienestar, fertilizer distribution) in response to food price inflation, but total spending on these programs was limited at around 0.3% of GDP, with potential efficacy concerns.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"mixed","actor":"Mexican government","action":"scaled up pre-existing agricultural support programs to address food price inflation","mechanism":"financial incentives for sustainable farming; price guarantees; fertilizer distribution; milk subsidies; subsidized food at Diconsa stores","outcome":"Government had instruments to react quickly but scale was limited; Sembrando Vida's dual objectives (poverty reduction and food supply) may conflict, and land ownership requirement may exclude the poorest","dates":["2019 (Sembrando Vida launch)","2022 (scale-up)"],"quantities":["~0.3% of GDP for pre-existing household food policies","Fertilizer program extended to 9 states from 5"],"excerpt":"The focus on pre-existing policies has provided the government with instruments to react relatively quickly to price pressures; however, the scale of these policies is somewhat limited at around 0.3 percent of GDP.","locator":"page 75","attribution":"IMF Staff Report, Mexico Article IV Consultation","period_fit":"Scale-up occurred in 2022.","source_limitations":["Lack of clarity on policy objectives may hinder efficacy; Sembrando Vida's land ownership requirement likely excludes the poorest households; smaller farmer focus may not be optimal for boosting food supply"],"question_ids":["5B.6","5B.7","5B.8"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0008","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's manufacturing sector accounts for about one-fifth of GDP but explains three-fourths of Mexico's short-term GDP fluctuations, with a near one-to-one short-term association between Mexico's manufacturing exports and U.S. production.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"Mexican manufacturing sector","action":"responded to U.S. demand fluctuations with near one-to-one correlation","mechanism":"deep trade integration via NAFTA; manufacturing exports tied to U.S. business cycle","outcome":"Manufacturing sector disproportionately drives Mexico's GDP volatility despite being only ~20% of GDP","dates":[],"quantities":["~1/5 of GDP","~3/4 of short-term GDP fluctuations","1-to-1 short-term association with U.S. manufacturing production"],"excerpt":"Even though the manufacturing sector accounts for only one-fifth of GDP, it explains about three-fourths of Mexico's short-term GDP fluctuations. Production in this sector is much more reactive to short-term developments than production elsewhere in the economy. In fact, there is a one-to-one short-term association between Mexico's manufacturing exports and production in the U.S.","locator":"page 76","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and INEGI data","period_fit":"Time-varying analysis uses rolling 12-year windows; covers NAFTA period (mid-90s) through 2022.","source_limitations":["Rolling regression estimates with Newey-West estimator; confidence bands shown at 90% level","Post-pandemic recovery may represent a temporary boost from U.S. shift from services to goods"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0009","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"A 1% change in U.S. GDP growth was associated with a 1.5% change in Mexico GDP growth in the 2010s, compared to about 0.2% in the 1980s, reflecting increased economic integration through NAFTA.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"context","actor":"U.S. economy / Mexican economy","action":"transmitted growth fluctuations from U.S. to Mexico via trade and manufacturing integration","mechanism":"NAFTA-driven trade integration; manufacturing sector as transmission channel","outcome":"Mexico's business cycle became much more sensitive to U.S. fluctuations over time","dates":["1980s (0.2% association)","2010s (1.5% association)"],"quantities":["1.5% change in Mexico GDP per 1% change in US GDP in 2010s","0.2% change in Mexico GDP per 1% change in US GDP in 1980s"],"excerpt":"A one-percent change in U.S. GDP was associated with a 1.5 percent change in Mexico GDP in the 2010s, compared to about 0.2 percent in the 1980s.","locator":"page 76","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis and INEGI data","period_fit":"Rolling window regression analysis covers the full period.","source_limitations":["12-year rolling window regressions; confidence bands at 90%; during post-pandemic recovery, Mexico benefited from U.S. shift from services to goods but demand composition expected to normalize"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0010","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Remittances increased during the Global Financial Crisis and COVID-19 pandemic, demonstrating a countercyclical pattern that provided support to the Mexican economy during U.S. downturns.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican workers remitting from the U.S.","action":"sent increased remittances during U.S. economic crises","mechanism":"Countercyclical support; GFC increase partly from dollar appreciation boosting peso value of transfers; COVID increase may reflect efforts to support relatives in Mexico","outcome":"Countercyclical remittance flows partially offset negative GDP effects of U.S. recessions on Mexico","dates":["2008-2009 (GFC)","2020-2021 (COVID-19)"],"quantities":["GFC: remittances increased during U.S. recession","COVID-19: remittances rose to almost 4% of GDP in 2021 from slightly less than 1% in 2000"],"excerpt":"By contrast, remittances seem to be countercyclical; they were increasing in both the GFC and the COVID-19 pandemic.","locator":"page 77","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using U.S. Bureau of Economic Analysis, INEGI, and Banxico data","period_fit":"Covers 2000-2021 period.","source_limitations":["During COVID-19 with travel restrictions, the reported boom may partly reflect replacement of cash transfers by wire transfers which can be better observed"],"question_ids":["5B.9","5B.10"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0011","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Mexico's exports to the U.S. increased by approximately USD 0.85 billion (0.07 percentage points of 2012 GDP) following U.S. sanctions on Russia in 2014, suggesting positive trade diversion effects for Mexico.","claim_type":"observed_fact","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican exporters / U.S. importers","action":"increased exports to the United States after U.S. sanctions on Russia","mechanism":"Trade diversion; U.S. importers shifted away from Russian goods toward Mexican suppliers","outcome":"Mexico gained approximately USD 0.85 billion in exports to the U.S.","dates":["2015-16 comparison period after March and December 2014 sanctions"],"quantities":["USD 0.85 billion increase","0.07 percentage points of 2012 GDP","1.99% to 2.06% of 2012 GDP for US imports from Mexico"],"excerpt":"Mexico's exports to the U.S. have increased after sanctions by about USD 0.85 billion or 0.07 percentage points of 2012 GDP, comparing imports of 2015-16 to 2012-14.","locator":"page 78","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using UN Comtrade and USITC data","period_fit":"Event study covers 2012-2016, with shock dates in March and December 2014.","source_limitations":["Analysis does not attribute causality; could capture other time-varying effects besides sanctions; local projections using shock dummies for executive order months mitigates but does not eliminate this concern"],"question_ids":["5B.1","5B.4"],"verification_status":"pending","premium_verification_required":false},{"draft_id":"D0012","source_id":"MAC-010","claim":"Dynamic regression analysis showed statistically significant positive effects on Mexico's exports to the U.S. following the March and December 2014 U.S. sanctions on Russia, with coefficients on time dummy variables increasing in the months following the sanctions.","claim_type":"source_assertion","polarity":"favorable","actor":"Mexican exporters","action":"increased exports to the U.S. following 2014 Russia sanctions","mechanism":"Trade diversion from Russia to Mexico as U.S. shifted sourcing","outcome":"Time dummy coefficients increased in months following March and December 2014 U.S. sanctions on Russia","dates":["March 2014 and December 2014 (U.S. executive orders against Russia)"],"quantities":[],"excerpt":"The coefficient of the time dummy increases in the months following the U.S. sanctions in March and December 2014, suggesting positive effects on Mexico's exports after the sanctions.","locator":"page 78","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using UN Comtrade and USITC data, monthly HS 6-digit level imports","period_fit":"Regression covers 2012-2016 period.","source_limitations":["Regresses log of nominal U.S. imports on time dummies, U.S. tariffs to Mexico at product level, and product fixed effects; local projection model with 3 lags of dependent variable, shock dummies, GDP, and tariffs","outcome":"Mexico's nominal exports to the U.S. increased by approximately 10% four months after the sanction shock","dates":["4 months after March and December 2014 U.S. sanctions on Russia"],"quantities":["~10% increase in nominal exports 4 months after shock"],"excerpt":"The impulse responses suggest a positive statistically significant effect with nominal exports from Mexico increasing by about 10 percent four months after the sanction.","locator":"page 78","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations using UN Comtrade and USITC data","period_fit":"Local projection covers 2012-2016 with shocks for March and December 2014 executive orders.","source_limitations":["Could capture other time-varying effects; pass-through to domestic prices","outcome":"Food prices constituted roughly 50% of inflation overshoot above Banxico's target range, larger role than in many peer countries","dates":["2021-2022 (current surge)","2008, 2011-13, 2017-18 (prior episodes)"],"quantities":["~50% of inflation increase above upper limit attributable to food prices"],"excerpt":"An important difference is the greater role of food prices in the inflation surge in Mexico, contributing roughly half of the increase in inflation above the upper limit of Banxico's inflation target range.","locator":"page 80","attribution":"IMF Staff calculations, as cited in IMF Staff Report","period_fit":"Current surge covers 2021-2022;
